sentences: We also find something like my warning in the New & Old Testaments.
Ecclesiastes 5:4–6 says it is better not to make a vow than to make one and fail to keep it.
If you tell the priest you didn’t mean what you promised, the passage warns that God will be angry and destroy your work.
Matthew 5:33–37 and James 5:12 are stranger still beside wedding vows: let your “Yes” be “Yes” and your “No” be “No,” and anything beyond that comes from evil.
A wedding vow is exactly that kind of extra promise, and to me that makes it look suspicious.
If your yes is trustworthy, why does it need another layer?

haiku: Both blocks follow the same shape (a scripture reference, what it says, then a short closing turn), and the sentences are of similar length and cleanly built, which reads more machine-made than a loose human draft would. Still, one paragraph cannot establish authorship, and the voice carries a personal stake and concrete detail, so it reads as a mixed, edited human-style passage more than as plainly generated text.
sonnet: The build is very regular. Each of the two paragraphs gives a citation, a paraphrase, and then a framing comment, and the second one ends on a rhetorical question. The rhythm is even, with mid-length sentences and no digressions, so it reads like a polished explainer. The evidence for AI polish is modest, and the first-person stance and the odd specifics keep it from reading as fully machine-made.
